extracted.intended_audience: amateur aviators, experimenters, and builders of gliders and model aeroplanes
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and safety/construction standards for building, balancing, launching, towing, and flying a 20-foot bi-plane glider (and models) aimed at early aviators and hobbyist experimenters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid flying in strong winds / broken ground
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attempt gliding over ground broken by trees or other natural objects or when the wind is blowing over 12-15 miles per hour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eddy currents form around obstacles and in high winds; these produce rising and falling currents that can unpredictably lift or drop one end of the machine. Avoid slopes with nearby protruding objects and do not fly when wind exceeds ~12–15 mph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not launch from precipitous cliffs or buildings
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not under any consideration jump off from a height which rises prominently from surrounding objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Otto Lilienthal warned against starting glides from high cliffs/buildings because gusts rebound from sides and strike the machine (hard to counteract) and the operator/machine are suddenly suspended high in the air — increasing risk. Prefer gradual launch sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive training: start on level ground and short jumps
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin by running against the wind on level ground and making short jumps; after practice transfer to a gentle slope to increase glide length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not be impatient; gradual progression greatly reduces danger. The Wright brothers practiced extensively with short flights before powered flight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always glide into the wind
rubrics_metrics.description: A gust from the front accelerates vertical motion (causing higher rise if already rising); a gust from the rear causes sudden drop—therefore always glide into the wind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan launches and landings so the machine faces and moves into the wind to reduce sudden drops and maintain control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equilibrium: centre of gravity alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: A glider remains in equilibrium only so long as the centre of gravity of the machine and operator fall in the same vertical line as the pressure exerted by the air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If centre of gravity is forward of pressure, the machine will incline forward and descend; if behind, the nose will rise; off-centre left/right causes leaning/turning. Design and loading must place CG appropriately relative to aerodynamic centre/centre of pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centre of pressure ahead of geometric centre
rubrics_metrics.description: The centre of pressure on the plane is somewhat in advance of the actual dimensional centre of the plane due to curvature and the disturbing action of the front edge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for the forward shift of pressure when setting centre of gravity and control surface positions; curvature and leading edge effects move effective lift forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing and control by shifting body/legs
rubrics_metrics.description: Balancing is accomplished in flight by moving the legs and body towards the side which is highest; shifting the centre of gravity by swinging the legs forward or moving the body alters pitch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small pilot body movements are primary control inputs for early gliders; moving forward causes descent (dips), moving back raises the nose (ascend). Avoid leaving weight too far rearward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of balancing (movable) small planes for roll control
rubrics_metrics.description: Small balancing planes mid-way between the main surfaces at each end are tilted by pilot foot-operated linkage to force down the high side and up the low side, restoring level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pilot presses down the end of the control bar on the high side, creating a negative angle on that balancing plane and a positive on the other — resulting in corrective roll. After practice this becomes almost automatic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action of aeroplane: lift by curved plane deflecting air downward
rubrics_metrics.description: The front edge of the aeroplane is elevated so the surfaces form an angle; the front edge enters still air and causes it to follow the curve and leave rearward/downwards; action and reaction produce lift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design supporting surfaces with appropriate curvature and angle of attack so moving bodies of air are deflected downward, producing upward reaction. Rapid motion means each parcel of air has little time to respond to inertia, aiding support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid eddy currents caused by obstacles and temperature changes
rubrics_metrics.description: When wind strikes natural objects streams divide producing rising currents on one side and falling currents on the other; temperature changes (e.g., sun behind clouds) also cause local rising/falling currents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These localized up/down drafts can abruptly raise or lower an end of the machine; do not attempt gliding near trees, stones or over thermally active surfaces. Observing surface water patterns (glassy streaks vs rough spots) can indicate rising/descending air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Launch technique: how to make a glide
rubrics_metrics.description: Carry the machine to the top of a slope, have assistants hold the lower plane ends, get in beneath, lift until arm sticks are under armpits, face the wind, elevate the front slightly, run a short distance and leap into the air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assistants can run a short distance to help but once in motion the pilot is relieved of weight and lift is felt. To land, push body towards back so the glider tips upward slightly in front, losing momentum and settling gently onto feet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Landing technique: rearward weight shift
rubrics_metrics.description: To land, push yourself towards the back of the machine so the glider tips upward slightly in front; it will then rise slightly, lose momentum and slowly settle so you drop gently on your feet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately shift CG rearward at the end of glide to reduce forward speed and soften landing. Avoid abrupt or excessive rearward movement that could stall the glider prematurely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Towed-flight parameters and behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: A glider attached to an automobile by a long bridle rises at a speed of between 15 and 20 miles per hour and remains in the air as long as the auto keeps moving at this rate; even when the towing automobile traveled about 50 mph the machine soared on a perfectly even keel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Towed launches require maintaining appropriate tow speed (typ. 15–20 mph for rise). Be aware of tow-line failures (wire broke in an example); the glider may still glide gently to ground if properly trimmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planform and dimensions for the described aeroplane
rubrics_metrics.description: Main supporting surfaces are five feet wide in the direction of flight and twenty-six feet long; curvature is segment of a parabola whose depth is one-ninth its length; planes are spaced vertically about four and one-half feet apart and converge slightly at the ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These dimensions and planform choices (span, chord, curvature ratio, interplane gap, tapered ends) are given as a successful configuration—use as starting design parameters but adjust for scale, weight, and loading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rib and fabric construction details
rubrics_metrics.description: Longitudinal curvature is maintained by spruce ribs half an inch square and spaced nine inches apart; fabric of close woven muslin over top and bottom fastened by grommets to a wire at rear ribs and by felt strips tacked to ribs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use light, strong materials and secure attachment methods to hold airfoil shape. Proper rib spacing and fabric fastening are critical to maintain curvature under aerodynamic loads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural framing and bracing using piano wire and turnbuckles
rubrics_metrics.description: All rectangles of structure are braced diagonally with steel piano wire; a small turnbuckle (nuclei made from bicycle spokes) is inserted in each brace to adjust length, forming a perfectly rigid truss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tensioned wire bracing with adjustable turnbuckles produces lightweight rigidity. Include accessible adjusters for preflight alignment and tensioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stanchion and spacing layout
rubrics_metrics.description: The stanchions are six feet apart except the middle two which are only eighteen inches apart; horizontal pieces of each surface are parallel and four feet distant from each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper placement of stanchions and interplane horizontal members maintains geometry and load distribution. Special closer spacing in the middle adds stiffness where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tail and control surface arrangement and sizes
rubrics_metrics.description: Ten feet rear of the main body is a horizontal tail, which halves a vertical rudder of about the same area; a front elevation rudder consists of two horizontal plane surfaces six feet by two feet turning about a transverse axis to alter angle to the wind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a movable vertical rudder for yaw (steered by the steering wheel) and a foreplane/elevator (6×2 ft) for pitch control linked to the steering wheel. The foreplane includes a central triangular fin to prevent unwanted turning from gusts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pilot seating, steering linkage, and control ergonomics
rubrics_metrics.description: Operator's seat is in front of supporting planes, carried on braces from the front wheel. Steering wheel mounted on a post hinged at the bottom; pushing/pulling the wheel controls elevation via a wooden rod connected to the steering post; rotating the wheel turns the movable vertical rudder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design control linkages so pilot can both adjust pitch (push/pull) and yaw (rotate) from the same interface. Ensure hinge, rod, and wheel placement provide reliable, easily reachable control inputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wheels and ground handling
rubrics_metrics.description: On the ground the machine runs on three twenty-inch pneumatic tired wheels (seamless rims, heavy motorcycle spokes); two under the rear edge of the lower plane, third wheel in advance of the body proper used when running on the ground prior to rising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use robust, pneumatic wheels sized for ground handling and takeoff roll; place wheels to support the machine during ground runs and initial lift-off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motor and propeller provisioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Motor (not yet installed in example) will be supported between the two main planes and connected to a laminated spruce propeller six feet in diameter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow structural provisions and clearances for a motor/propeller assembly between planes; choose a laminated spruce propeller of appropriate diameter and strength for anticipated power and loads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design against cross-gusts: converging ends and central fin
rubrics_metrics.description: The ends converge slightly to make the machine less affected by cross gusts; the elevation rudder has a triangular vertical plane through its middle to prevent turning by gusts striking the rear vertical rudder, neutralizing gust-induced turning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate geometric and aerodynamic features (tapered ends, central fins) to reduce susceptibility to asymmetric gusts and unwanted yaw/pitch coupling.
